title: Conveyor Safety Switches: 5 Lifesaving Types Explained
text:
Switches

 Conveyor Safety Switches: 5 Lifesaving Types Explained

 Pull cord, belt sway and zero speed switches stop a running belt before a small fault turns into an injury or a fire.

 
 Pull Cord Switch 
 Belt Sway Switch 
 Zero Speed Switch 
 Material Handling 
 




 Conveyor safety switches are field devices that detect dangerous conditions on a belt conveyor and trip the drive through the interlock circuit. The three most common are the pull cord switch, the belt sway switch and the zero speed switch.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to understand how conveyor safety switches work, which faults each one detects, and how they are wired into the conveyor interlock system.


 
 
 
 What Are Conveyor Safety Switches?


 Conveyor safety switches are rugged electromechanical or electronic devices mounted along a belt conveyor to detect unsafe conditions. When they operate, their contacts open the safety circuit and stop the drive motor, much like an emergency stop push button on a machine.


 Long conveyors in cement, steel, power, mining and port plants can run for hundreds of metres through unmanned galleries. A person, a misaligned belt or a slipping pulley can cause serious harm long before anyone in the control room notices.


 
 
 Image credit: Jayashree Electrodevices 
 

 These devices give every person along the belt a way to stop it and give the control system early warning of mechanical faults. Most are rated IP65 or IP66 because they live in dust, water spray and outdoor weather.


 The contacts are usually wired to a safety relay or a safety PLC input. This makes sure a single wiring fault does not hide a real trip.


 5 Types of Conveyor Protection Switches


 
 Pull Cord Switch
 A steel wire rope runs along the belt, and pulling it anywhere trips and latches the switch.
 Best for: emergency stopping by personnel
 Emergency Stop 

 Belt Sway Switch
 A roller lever touches the belt edge and trips when the belt drifts too far sideways.
 Best for: belt misalignment protection
 Alignment 

 Zero Speed Switch
 A sensor watches pulley rotation and trips if speed drops below a set value.
 Best for: belt slip and breakage
 Speed 

 Chute Jam Switch
 A tilt or probe switch detects material piling up in a transfer chute.
 Best for: blocked transfer points
 Blockage 

 Belt Rip Detector
 Detects longitudinal tears by sensing material falling through the belt.
 Best for: high value long belts
 Belt Damage 




 The first three are found on almost every belt and are the focus of this article. Chute jam and rip detectors are added where the risk or belt value justifies the cost.


 Mechanically, many of these devices are close cousins of the limit switch . The difference is the heavy duty actuator designed for belt duty.


 Pull Cord Switch Working


 
 Wire Rope Runs along the walkway at hand height

 Pull Anywhere Operator pulls the rope in an emergency

 Switch Trips Cam turns and contacts open

 Latch Holds Switch stays tripped with a visible flag

 Manual Reset Reset only by hand at that switch




 Switches are fitted on both sides of the conveyor, with rope running between them at hand height. Eaton specifies that the distance between two trip switches must not exceed 100 metres.


 The switch latches after it trips, so the belt cannot restart until someone walks to it and resets it by hand. This forces the operator to check the reason for the stop.


 This latching behaviour matches the emergency stop principle in ISO 13850. Our article on emergency stop and emergency power off explains the difference between the two stop categories.


 Belt Sway and Zero Speed Switches


 A belt sway switch has a vertical roller lever mounted close to the belt edge on both sides. If the belt tracks off centre, it pushes the lever and the cam operates the contacts.


 Two stage versions give an alarm at a small deflection and a trip at a larger one. One manufacturer lists a trip point of 17 degrees for a single stage unit, so always set angles from the datasheet.


 A zero speed switch watches the tail or bend pulley, which is driven by the belt rather than the motor. Most use an inductive proximity sensor or a magnetic pickup that counts pulses from a target on the shaft.


 If the belt slips on the drive pulley or breaks, the tail pulley slows down while the motor keeps running. The switch compares the pulse rate with a set point and trips after a start up delay.


 Zero Speed Switch Set Point Formula


 
 N = (v × 60) ÷ (π × D) 
 Trip speed = N × underspeed percent 

N = pulley speed in rpm
v = belt speed in m/s
D = pulley diameter in m

Worked example:
v = 2.5 m/s, D = 0.5 m
N = (2.5 × 60) ÷ (3.1416 × 0.5) = 150 ÷ 1.571 = 95.5 rpm
Underspeed trip at 80 percent
 Trip speed = 95.5 × 0.8 = 76.4 rpm 



 Set the underspeed point low enough to ignore normal load swings but high enough to catch real slip. Values between 70 and 90 percent of normal speed are common.


 On conveyors with a VFD , the normal speed changes with the drive set point. In that case the PLC should scale the trip limit to the commanded speed.


 4 Steps After a Pull Cord Trip


 
 1
 Locate the Switch
 Find the tripped unit using the flag or the trip indication panel.


 2
 Find the Cause
 Check for a person, jammed material or damage near that point.


 3
 Reset by Hand
 Reset the lever at the switch once the area is safe.


 4
 Restart Safely
 Sound the prestart warning and restart from the control room.





 For maintenance work, a pull cord stop is never a substitute for isolation. Always follow lockout tagout before anyone enters the belt area.


 Many plants fit a trip indication system that shows which switch operated. This saves long walks along galleries that can exceed a kilometre.
